title: E911 and RedSky
blurb: Dispatchable location, HELD, RedSky, Intrado, 933, and the callback number.

lessons.title: Kari's Law and RAY BAUM's Act
lessons.summary: US multi-line systems have federal 911 obligations. The FCC page is the source. This lab does not paraphrase the statute into new requirements.
objectives: Define dispatchable location in Cisco's words

diagram.caption: The FCC's MLTS page is the legal source. Cisco's article is the product source.

sections.h: What Cisco says you must be able to send
paragraphs: The emergency article describes routing to the right PSAP with a dispatchable location, and it names RedSky as the service used for that on Webex Calling.
Intrado is also documented later in the same article as a provider. The legal obligation does not name a vendor. The product article does.

lessons.title: PIDF-LO and HELD
lessons.summary: PIDF-LO is the location object. HELD is how a device asks a location server. Cisco maps those ideas onto MPP phones and the Webex App.
objectives: List what an MPP phone sends

diagram.caption: The phone asks with HELD. The location rides as PIDF-LO.

flow.title: A phone learns where it is

steps.label: See LLDP, BSSID, or IP
steps.detail: The article lists what HELD MPP phones report: LLDP switch, wireless BSSID, IP, or MAC.

steps.label: HELD request
steps.detail: HTTPS to the hosts the article names, port 443.

steps.label: Find the location
steps.detail: If the network element is known, the dispatchable location comes back.
steps.inspect: Unknown network is a different path

steps.label: Carry it
steps.detail: PIDF-LO is the location object format. RFC 4119.

paragraphs: The article's table says HELD is used by MPP phones and HELD+ by the Webex App. HELD+ adds the network wiremap path for the app.
Cisco Discovery Protocol is not supported for the app's HELD+ discovery. LLDP is. A phone in the middle of a pass-through port stops LLDP.

lessons.title: Enable a location
lessons.summary: RedSky ties to the organization with a HELD company ID and secret. The service is turned on per location. The US entitlement and the Canada license are not the same sentence.

diagram.caption: Company ID in Control Hub. Enablement on the location. 933 before you promise live 911.

steps.label: Copy the HELD company ID and secret
steps.detail: They correlate this organization to the RedSky customer. Cisco says it does not store your portal password. The wizard uses credentials once to obtain the ID.

steps.label: Match them
steps.detail: A mismatch warns you. Proceeding overwrites the previous account.

steps.label: Enable
steps.detail: US or Canada locations. International stays on PSTN emergency.

steps.label: Test
steps.detail: Confirm the address. The article tells you to do this before routing live emergency calls.

paragraphs: Automatic location configuration in the E911 portal is off by default for Webex Calling customers and on by default for Webex Wholesale.
Deleting a location does not delete the RedSky building.

cite.label: Enhanced emergency calling for Webex Calling

paragraphs: US Webex Calling users are entitled to the RedSky service with their calling entitlement, per the requirements table.
Canada: obtain the RedSky license through Cisco or the partner. Do not collapse those sentences.

lessons.title: HELD phones, non-HELD phones, and the app
lessons.summary: MPP phones and the Webex App can do dynamic location. Many other phones are caller-ID located. Moving them without an admin is how the PSAP gets the old building.
objectives: Name HELD device families from the article
Treat the rest as caller-ID devices

diagram.caption: Dynamic for HELD. Static caller ID for the rest.

steps.label: Mark HELD models
steps.detail: The article lists 9800 desk phones, 6800/7800/8800 MPP, the 7832 and 8832 MPP conference phones, DECT 6800 MPP, and ATA 191 and 192 among HELD-capable devices.
steps.inspect: Check the live supported-device list too

steps.label: Caller ID
steps.detail: Poly and Yealink models in the article's non-HELD list use the caller-ID address.

steps.label: Push config
steps.detail: Until the phone picks up HELD config, it does not use HELD. The article says that can take the next 24-hour check.

steps.label: Off-net prompt
steps.detail: The Webex App asks for an address when the network is unknown, for users off premises.
steps.inspect: Red X if they dismiss the need

paragraphs: Device management pushes HELD configuration after the location is enabled. If you do not resync, the phone may wait until its next configuration check, which the article bounds as within 24 hours.
A cutover on Friday afternoon without a resync is a weekend of caller-ID locations.

cite.label: Enhanced emergency calling for Webex Calling

paragraphs: HELD-capable MPP phones do not let the user hang up an emergency call. The far end releases it. If the far end does not, the article says a phone reset is the last option.
Tell the help desk before the first false 911.

cite.label: Enhanced emergency calling for Webex Calling

lessons.title: Nomadic users and the red X
lessons.summary: The Webex App updates location from the network when it can, and asks the user when it cannot. A signed-in user who roams may only see a red X.
lessons.uncertainty: The BroadWorks emergency article mentions a client configuration tag for prompt frequency. This lesson does not apply that tag to Webex Calling multi-tenant unless the Webex Calling article you are reading names it.

diagram.caption: Unknown network: prompt at sign-in, red X if they were already signed in.

steps.label: Update silently
steps.detail: If RedSky knows the network, the article says the location updates automatically.

steps.label: Prompt
steps.detail: The user enters an address. RedSky validates and stores it.

steps.label: Red X
steps.detail: The article says they are not prompted in that case. They click the red X.

steps.label: Native dialer
steps.detail: A soft client with cellular capability hands the emergency call to the phone. Webex never sees it.

paragraphs: Ignoring the red X means the next emergency call can use a stale address. The article describes that indicator in the footer.
This is a training problem as much as a network problem.

paragraphs: There is no Webex call record and no Webex ECBN.
Do not debug a missing CDR for a mobile 911 that the OS placed.

fault.title: Ignored red X
fault.symptom: A traveler calls 911 and the PSAP is sent to yesterday's office.

lessons.title: Intrado beside RedSky

steps.detail: The article supports both. The contract picks one.
steps.inspect: Do not enable both by experiment

steps.label: Copy that provider's ID
steps.detail: Intrado's labels in the article are Company ID (Account ID) and Secret Key (HELD WEBEX).

steps.label: Test

paragraphs: The Intrado confirmation text says misconfiguration can send calls to a relay center and that additional charges can apply.
That sentence is why 933 exists.

Use the alerts. They are how you see nomadic users without waiting for a real emergency.

lessons.title: Emergency review
lessons.summary: A location is ready when the provider, the wiremap or caller-ID address, the resync, the ECBN, and a 933 result all exist.

diagram.caption: Five pieces of evidence. A toggle is only one.

steps.detail: RedSky or Intrado, right company ID.

steps.label: Classified
steps.detail: HELD resynced. Caller-ID phones have a static address.

steps.label: Per location
steps.detail: The address matches the floor.

steps.label: Callable
steps.detail: One of the three documented choices, and someone answers.

paragraphs: Do not fail a UK site for lacking RedSky. The article says international emergency stays on the PSTN.
Do fail it for having no PSTN emergency test of its own.

fault.title: ECBN to a closed attendant
fault.symptom: 933 showed the right floor. The PSAP callback reached a menu that hangs up after hours.
fault.cause: The address was right and the callback number was not answerable.
fault.fix: Point ECBN at a line that answers, including after hours, and place the carrier's callback test.
